senses.definition: An itchy feeling resembling the result of tickling.
examples: I have a persistent tickle in my throat.

senses.definition: (cricket, informal) A light tap of the ball.

quotes.text: There's a very fine line between a tickle and an edge!

senses.definition: (Newfoundland) A narrow strait, such as between an island and the shore.

quotes.text: Charts and Plans. [...] No. New Charts. 2253 England, and south coast—Dartmouth harbour. [...] 3320 Newfoundland, Thimble tickles and Glover harbour—Head of Seal bay.
quotes.reference: 1903 April 8, The Syren and Shipping, page 169:

quotes.text: Cow Head itself is a prominent headland connected to the settlement by a natural causeway, or ‘tickle’ as the Newfoundlanders prefer it.
quotes.reference: 2004, Richard Fortey, The Earth, Folio Society, published 2011, page 169:

senses.definition: (transitive) To touch repeatedly or stroke delicately in a manner which typically causes laughter, pleasure and twitching.
examples: He tickled Nancy's tummy, and she started to giggle.

quotes.text: If you tickle us, do we not laugh?
quotes.reference: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London: […] Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene i]:

senses.definition: (intransitive, of a body part) To feel as if the body part in question is being tickled.
examples: My nose tickles, and I'm going to sneeze!

senses.definition: (transitive) To appeal to someone's taste, curiosity etc.
(transitive) To cause delight or amusement in.
examples: He was tickled to receive such a wonderful gift.

quotes.text:
Behold the child, by Nature's kindly law,
Pleas'd with a rattle, tickled with a straw.
quotes.reference: 1733, Alexander Pope, “Epistle II”, in An Essay on Man, lines 275–276; republished in The Complete Poetical Works of Alexander Pope, Boston, New York: Houghton, Mifflin and Company, 1902, page 145:

quotes.text:
Such a nature
Tickled with good success, disdains the shadow
Which he treads on at noon.
quotes.reference: c. 1608–1609 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedy of Coriolanus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London: […] Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene i]:

quotes.text:
He with secret joy therefore
Did tickle inwardly in every vein.
quotes.reference: 1591, Ed[mund] Sp[enser], “Muiopotmos, or The Fate of the Butterflie”, in Complaints. Containing Sundrie Small Poemes of the Worlds Vanitie. […], London: […] William Ponsonbie, […], →OCLC:

senses.definition: (transitive) To catch fish in the hand (usually in rivers or smaller streams) by manually stimulating the fins.

quotes.text:

Lucio. I warrant it is: And thy head stands so tickle on
thy shoulders, that a milke-maid, if she be in loue, may
sigh it off: Send after the Duke, and appeale to him.
